# Estimation and comparing models {#estimation}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* describe marginal maximum likelihood estimation in words;
* check whether a model has converged, and know what to do when it has not;
* compare nested models with a likelihood-ratio test and any models with
  information criteria;
* judge overall model fit with M2, RMSEA, SRMSR and CFI;
* explain why AIC and BIC can disagree, and what sample size has to do with
  it.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[calibration](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#calibration),
[marginal maximum likelihood](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#marginal-maximum-likelihood),
[convergence](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#convergence),
[standard error](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#standard-error),
[likelihood-ratio test](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#likelihood-ratio-test),
[information criteria](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#information-criteria),
[M2](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#m2),
[RMSEA](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#rmsea),
[SRMSR](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#srmsr),
[CFI and TLI](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#cfi-tli).

## The ideas

**Calibration** means estimating the item parameters. We never observe
$\theta$, so we cannot simply regress responses on it. **Marginal maximum
likelihood** (MML) instead assumes a distribution for $\theta$ in the
population, usually standard normal, and integrates it out: The likelihood
of a response pattern is its probability averaged over all possible values
of $\theta$. The item parameters are chosen to make the observed patterns as
likely as possible [@bock1981].

mirt maximizes this likelihood with the **EM algorithm** by default. It
replaces the integral with a sum over a grid of *quadrature points* and
alternates two steps: The E-step works out, for every person, how likely each
grid point is given their responses and the current item parameters; the
M-step updates each item's parameters as if those expected counts were
data. The cycles stop when the parameters stop changing, which is called
**convergence**. If the algorithm hits its limit of 500 cycles first, mirt
warns you, and the estimates should not be trusted.

Once a model has converged, we compare it with alternatives.

* **Likelihood-ratio test (LRT).** For *nested* models (the Rasch model is a
  2PL with equal slopes; the 2PL is a 3PL with $c = 0$), twice the difference
  in log-likelihoods is approximately chi-square distributed with degrees of
  freedom equal to the difference in the number of parameters. With large
  samples even trivial improvements become significant.
* **Information criteria.** $\text{AIC} = -2\log L + 2k$ and
  $\text{BIC} = -2\log L + k\log N$, where $k$ is the number of parameters
  and $N$ the sample size. Smaller is better. BIC punishes extra parameters
  more heavily once $N > 7$, so it favours simpler models. A difference of 10
  or more BIC points is usually read as strong evidence.
* **Absolute fit.** The **M2** statistic [@maydeu2006] compares observed and
  expected proportions for single items and pairs of items. RMSEA (below
  about 0.05 is close fit), SRMSR (below about 0.05) and CFI (above about 0.95)
  are effect sizes built from it. Treat the cut-offs as rough guides, not
  rules.

## Example 1: A test the Rasch model fits

`LSAT6` is another five-item section of the Law School Admission Test, with
1,000 test takers. It is a textbook example of data the Rasch model fits well.

```{r data-estimation-1}
# Five dichotomous LSAT items, one row per test taker.
resp <- expand.table(LSAT6)
```

Fit the models one at a time, check convergence, and compare them:

```{r}
rasch <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
twopl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
extract.mirt(rasch, "converged")
extract.mirt(twopl, "iterations")
anova(rasch, twopl)
```

The 2PL improves the log-likelihood by a fraction of a point for four extra
parameters, so the LRT is far from significant and both AIC and BIC prefer
the Rasch model. `glance()` adds the absolute fit statistics:

```{r}
glance(rasch)[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC", "M2", "df", "p.value", "RMSEA", "SRMSR", "CFI")]
```

`select_model()` runs all of this in one call. It fits the Rasch, 2PL and
3PL models (or the polytomous equivalents), checks convergence, ranks them by
BIC, runs the LRTs between nested pairs and explains its recommendation.

```{r}
sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE)
sel
```

```{r select-plot, fig.height = 2.6, fig.cap = "Model comparison for LSAT6: each model's information criterion relative to the best model (0 = best)."}
autoplot(sel)
```

The `weight` column converts BIC differences into the relative support for
each model; here nearly all of it goes to the Rasch model.

## Example 2: When the criteria disagree

Now take the 32 science items of `SAT12`, scored with the corrected key from
Chapter \@ref(measurement).

```{r data-estimation-2}
# SAT12 science items, scored with the corrected key (item 32 keyed 3).
key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,3)
resp <- key2binary(SAT12, key)
```

```{r}
sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE)
sel
sel$lrt
```

This time the evidence is mixed. The LRT and AIC prefer the 3PL, while BIC
prefers the 2PL. Neither is "wrong": They answer different questions. The
LRT asks whether the extra 32 guessing parameters improve fit beyond chance,
and with 600 people the answer is yes. BIC asks which model is more likely to
be the better description once we account for the cost of 32 more
parameters, and it says the 2PL. A sensible report states the tension and
the reason for the final choice: If scores will be used for decisions about
low-scoring students, where guessing matters most, the 3PL may be worth its
cost; for a short research scale, the 2PL is easier to defend.

### Small samples and convergence

The 3PL is the hardest of the three to estimate, because the lower
asymptote is determined only by what low-ability people do. With 200 students
the EM algorithm may not converge at all:

```{r}
set.seed(303)
small <- resp[sample(nrow(resp), 200), ]
fit_small <- mirt(small, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE)
extract.mirt(fit_small, "converged")
summary(coef(fit_small, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"])
```

Some lower asymptotes drift to zero and others to implausibly large values.
Three common remedies are to use a 2PL, to fix $c$ at a sensible value (for
five-option items, 0.2), or to put a **prior** on $c$ so that the data only
move it away from a plausible value when they have something to say. In mirt
a prior is part of the model syntax. Here a beta(5, 17) prior centres $c$
near 0.2 (`expbeta` applies it on the scale mirt uses internally):

```{r}
spec <- mirt.model("F = 1-32
                    PRIOR = (1-32, g, expbeta, 5, 17)")
fit_prior <- mirt(small, spec, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE)
extract.mirt(fit_prior, "converged")
summary(coef(fit_prior, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"])
```

With the prior the model converges and the lower asymptotes stay in a
believable range. Report priors when you use them: They are part of the
model.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. For `LSAT6`, compute the LRT statistic for Rasch versus 2PL by hand from
   the two log-likelihoods, and check it against `anova()`.
2. Fit the 2PL to `SAT12` with `quadpts = 15` and with the default of 61
   points. Do the item parameters change? What does that tell you?
3. Draw 300 students from `SAT12` and rerun `select_model()`. Does the
   recommendation change? Repeat with another random sample.
4. A colleague reports "the 3PL fitted significantly better (p < .001), so we
   used it". What would you ask them?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
ll <- c(extract.mirt(rasch, "logLik"), extract.mirt(twopl, "logLik"))
lrt <- 2 * (ll[2] - ll[1])
c(X2 = lrt, df = 4, p = pchisq(lrt, 4, lower.tail = FALSE))

m15 <- mirt(resp, 1, "2PL", quadpts = 15, verbose = FALSE)
m61 <- mirt(resp, 1, "2PL", quadpts = 61, verbose = FALSE)
max(abs(coef(m15, simplify = TRUE)$items - coef(m61, simplify = TRUE)$items))
```

2. With only 15 points some estimates move by about 0.1 on the
   slope-intercept scale; between 61 (the default for one dimension) and more
   points they hardly move at all. Fewer points trade accuracy for speed,
   which matters mainly for models with several dimensions.
3. With fewer people, BIC's penalty matters relatively more and the
   likelihood gains of the 3PL are smaller, so the 2PL (or even the Rasch
   model) is chosen more often. Model choice depends on the sample, not only
   on the items.
4. Did the model converge? What did BIC say? How large is the sample? Are the
   guessing estimates plausible, and what were their standard errors? Would
   the scores or decisions differ between the 2PL and the 3PL?

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Bock and Aitkin [-@bock1981] introduced the EM approach to marginal maximum
likelihood. Maydeu-Olivares and Joe [-@maydeu2006] describe M2. de Ayala
[-@deayala2022] discusses model comparison and fit in detail.
